title: Several infrastructure projects put on backburner as ACT 'at peak construction'
description: Some ACT government infrastructure projects, including health, emergency services and sports facilities in North Gungahlin, will be deferred to save about $700 million over four years.
content_snippet: Infrastructure projects that aren't ready to be built or already under construction will be put on the backburner or broken into stages under an ACT government plan to save $700 million over the next…
author: Harry Frost
full_text: ACT government to put some infrastructure projects on backburner to help relieve budget pressure Sun 7 Jun 2026 at 7:00pm In short: Several ACT government infrastructure projects will be put on the backburner, while others will be broken into stages to reduce budget pressure. Details of exactly which projects will be affected will be confirmed in Wednesday's budget, but Chief Minister Andrew Barr says the adjustments are expected to save the government $700 million over four years. What's next? Mr Barr insists the government will keep its election commitments and projects will still start during the current parliamentary term, but not necessarily in the coming financial year. Infrastructure projects that aren't ready to be built or already under construction will be put on the backburner or broken into stages under an ACT government plan to save $700 million over the next four years. The adjustments to the government's infrastructure program, to be confirmed in Wednesday's territory budget, will prioritise health and housing supply projects including the new Northside Hospital at Bruce and the delivery of public and affordable housing. Some projects will be "deferred", including health, emergency services and sports facilities in North Gungahlin, to prioritise completion of other projects, including outdoor sports facilities like the Taylor District Playing Fields and Tennis Facility, as well as the Belconnen Basketball Stadium redevelopment. ACT Chief Minister Andrew Barr insists the government will keep its election commitments and projects will still commence during the current parliamentary term, but not necessarily in the coming financial year. "We're not scrapping projects, but we just need to get the current backlog finished before we can start new work,"Mr Barr said. "The community's number one priority in all of the feedback to government is the health sector. "So that's why there is a very strong focus not only on the Northside Hospital, but on community health facilities. "During the COVID period, we did ramp up the infrastructure program with a view to support the economy through that pretty difficult period. "But that's not a sustainable level of infrastructure spend into the future, and so we will be returning to a more normal level of infrastructure. "What that means is less than a billion dollars a year." An emergency services station promised in Casey is among projects to be deferred. "The priority for emergency services at this point has been getting the Molonglo station open and staffed," Mr Barr said. "And then on the police side, the City Police Station and the new headquarters. "The Casey facility will come, we're definitely committed to building it, it's just not going to be in this year's budget." 'We're at peak construction at the moment' Other projects, such as the long awaited Kingston Arts Precinct, will be "staged", with the initial land release to deliver structured car parking and artist housing in Kingston first, before additional arts facilities are built in later years. "We understand that some of the challenges in the city in recent times have been multiple projects being undertaken at once and that has impacted on car parking availability," Mr Barr said. "And so we would not seek to repeat that in Kingston. "Staging the development allows us to do that." In a report as part of an ACT Legislative Assembly inquiry into the territory's fiscal sustainability, independent economist Saul Eslake found the "significant deterioration" of the territory's fiscal position over the past decade was entirely attributable to "conscious policy decisions" made by the ACT government. But Mr Barr points to external factors for prompting the changes, such as labour shortages, supply chain issues from the war in the Middle East and the pending pressure on the construction sector from the 2032 Olympic Games in Brisbane. "I think we're at peak construction at the moment. There's only so many tradies, there's only so many bits of material available," Mr Barr said. "We're also impacted by decisions that are made in other jurisdictions around particular projects. "Now is definitely not the time to be trying to build the same sorts of things as are going to be built in Brisbane for [the Olympic Games]. "The workforce and the contractors, the big tier one companies who build these sorts of projects in Australia, are headed to Brisbane." Future infrastructure spending will increasingly focus on repairing and renewing aging assets rather than building entirely new facilities. "We've got really four sources of funding for our infrastructure: Commonwealth co-contributions, revenue we generate from asset sales, that's land in large part that we release for housing, and we reinvest the profits from that into the infrastructure for those areas," Mr Barr said. "We also have operating cash surpluses in good years that we can apply to infrastructure, and then the final source is borrowings. "And it is appropriate for some infrastructure that's going to serve the community for 50 to 100 years that the cost of building that infrastructure is spread over multiple generations. "You bring those four finance sources together and some projects will get Commonwealth funding." Light rail to Woden remains in the approvals, environmental assessment and design phase. Mr Barr said procurement could not begin until all approvals and detailed designs were complete. "I think we also need to settle on the preferred procurement methodology and one option that is being pursued is an availability public-private partnership,"he said. "That was the methodology we used to procure the first stage of light rail and in effect, what that is, is procuring not just the tracks but an entire service, and paying on performance and staging the payments over 20 years, which is how the first stage [between the city and Gungahlin] was procured. "That option is still there for us but we can't go to the market for that until we have all of the approvals and detailed design resolved." Changes expose 'reckless spending', opposition says The opposition says the government's decision to quietly announce changes to its infrastructure plan on a long weekend was an admission of "reckless spending" and "financial mismanagement". "They [The ACT government] don't want anyone to hear the news because it's a massive admission that they were wrong and we were right all along," Opposition Leader Mark Parton said. "It's an admission that their reckless spending on infrastructure projects is unsustainable. It's a sad reflection on the last 15 years of financial mismanagement and it's a signal of more to come. "If they're cutting things that are already in the forward estimates, how do you reckon we're looking with things that are not yet budgeted for?"
